\chapter{La cuenta}
\label{ch:es-cuenta}
\hlchaptermodality{456}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can order from a set menu and then read the bill: name a first course, tell a price from a charge, query something that was added, and ask whether they take cards.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la ensalada]{la ensalada — the salted thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C456-ensalada}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la sal} and \textbf{la verdura}. Put the first on the second and you have named a dish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ensalada}
\textbf{la ensalada} — the salad.

\emph{Una ensalada mixta} — a mixed salad, the standard one on every menu: lettuce, tomato, onion, tuna, olives. \emph{De primero, ensalada} — salad to start.

\textbf{Ensaladilla} is not a small salad. \emph{La ensaladilla rusa} is a cold dish of potato, carrot, tuna and mayonnaise, and it is a fixture in bars.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ordering a course}]
A set menu comes in courses, and Spanish names them with \textbf{de}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{what it covers} \\
\midrule
\emph{de primero} & for a first course \\
\emph{de segundo} & for a main \\
\emph{de postre} & for pudding \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{De primero, una ensalada} is a complete order. No verb is needed, and adding \emph{quiero} makes it heavier rather than politer — the waiter has asked what you are having for each course, and the phrase answers exactly that.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Ensalada} is \emph{en-} plus \emph{sal}: a thing that has been \textbf{salted}.

It came from Catalan or Occitan and reached English as \textbf{salad} through French, wearing the salt down to nothing on the way. Spanish kept it visible, which is the whole point of stopping here — the dish is named after the dressing, not after the leaves.

The same \textbf{sal} is in \textbf{la salsa}, a sauce, and in \textbf{el salario} — Latin \emph{salārium} is built on \emph{sal}, and that much is solid. The famous story attached to it is not: no Roman source says soldiers were paid in salt, and the salt lesson has already warned you that the tale is an eighteenth-century invention. A salad, a sauce and a salary share a root; they do not share that anecdote.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a mixed salad
  \item salad to start, using the phrase from the table above
  \item what \emph{ensalada}, \emph{salsa} and \emph{salario} share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The salad? (\textbf{La ensalada}.) For a first course? (\textbf{De primero}.) What is inside the word? (\textbf{Sal} — it is the salted thing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cargo]{el cargo — what has been put on the bill}

\label{lesson:ES-C456-cargo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el carrito} and \textbf{la cuenta}. A cart carries a load, and so does a bill.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el cargo}
\textbf{el cargo} — the charge: an amount put onto a bill or an account.

\emph{Hay un cargo de doce euros} — there's a twelve-euro charge. \emph{Un cargo por servicio} — a service charge. \emph{Sin cargo} — free of charge, the wording on a receipt.

\textbf{Cargar} is the verb — \emph{me han cargado dos veces}, they've charged me twice — and it also means to load, and to charge a phone.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: cargo is not precio}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you mean} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
what a thing costs & \textbf{el precio} \\
an amount added to your bill & \textbf{el cargo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El precio de la ensalada} is on the menu; \emph{un cargo en la cuenta} is something a business has placed there, and you may be querying it. That is why \emph{cargo} turns up on disputes and \emph{precio} does not: a \emph{precio} is announced in advance, a \emph{cargo} appears afterwards.

\emph{El cargo} has a third life as a post or office — \emph{el cargo de director} — for the same reason: a job is a load somebody carries.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{carricare}, to load a cart, built on \textbf{carrus} — the cart itself, which Spanish kept as \emph{el carro} and shrank into \textbf{el carrito}.

So a charge on your bill is a \textbf{load put onto a cart}, and the picture holds in every branch of the family: \textbf{la carga} is a load, \textbf{el cargamento} is cargo, and \textbf{descargar} is to unload — or to download, which is unloading onto your machine.

English has the same \emph{carricare} twice, by two different doors: \textbf{charge} came through French, and \textbf{cargo} was taken straight from Spanish in the seventeenth century. Two English words, one Latin verb, and one of them is this very Spanish noun.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item there's a twelve-euro charge on the bill
  \item free of charge
  \item which word is on the menu and which on the bill
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The charge? (\textbf{El cargo}.) Free of charge? (\textbf{Sin cargo}.) What was a \emph{carrus}? (\textbf{A cart} — the same one inside \emph{el carrito}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aceptar]{aceptar — we take that here}

\label{lesson:ES-C456-aceptar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{pagar} and \textbf{la cuenta}. The question is whether they take the card.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aceptar}
\textbf{aceptar} — to accept.

\begin{quote}
No se \textbf{aceptan} tarjetas.
\end{quote}

\emph{¿Aceptan tarjeta?} — do you take card? \emph{Acepto} — I accept, on a form or a screen. \emph{Aceptar las condiciones} — to accept the terms.

It is the verb of agreeing to something offered: money, terms, an invitation, an apology.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: aceptar is not admitir}]
Both come out as \textquotedblleft{}accept\textquotedblright{} in English and they part company on a bill:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what is happening} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
you agree to take what is offered & \textbf{aceptar} \\
you let something in, or own up to it & \textbf{admitir} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Aceptan tarjeta} — they will take your card. \emph{No se admiten perros} — dogs are not let in. And \emph{admitir un error} is to own up to one, where \emph{aceptar un error} would mean putting up with it.

The test is direction: \emph{aceptar} is about \textbf{agreeing}, \emph{admitir} about \textbf{letting through}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{accipere}: \textbf{ad-}, towards, plus \textbf{capere}, \textbf{to take}.

So to accept is to take a thing \textbf{towards yourself}, and the direction is the whole meaning. Something you did not take towards yourself, you did not accept.

\emph{Capere} is one of Latin's most productive verbs and you meet it constantly in English: \textbf{capture}, \textbf{capable}, \textbf{captive}, \textbf{receive} (\emph{re-capere}, take back), \textbf{deceive}, \textbf{conceive}, \textbf{perceive}. Spanish has \emph{capaz}, \emph{captar}, \emph{recibir} and \emph{percibir} from the same stem.

The \textbf{c} before \textbf{e} is soft, so \emph{aceptar} is \emph{a-thep-TAR} in Spain and \emph{a-sep-TAR} elsewhere — the same rule that gave you \emph{accidente}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item do you take card?
  \item cards are not accepted, as the sign puts it
  \item which verb fits a sign about dogs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To accept? (\textbf{Aceptar}.) What does \emph{capere} mean? (\textbf{To take}.) Which direction does the \emph{ad-} give it? (\textbf{Towards you}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el coste]{el coste — what it comes to}

\label{lesson:ES-C456-coste}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{costar} and \textbf{el precio}. The verb has a noun of its own, and it is not \emph{precio}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el coste}
\textbf{el coste} — the cost.

\emph{El coste total} — the total cost. \emph{El coste del envío} — the cost of postage. \emph{Sin coste adicional} — at no extra cost.

In Latin America you will more often hear \textbf{el costo}; Spain says \emph{coste}. Both are the noun sitting beside \emph{costar}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: coste, precio, cargo}]
Three words now stand between you and a bill you can read:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it names} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
what the seller asks & \textbf{el precio} \\
what it works out at for you & \textbf{el coste} \\
an amount added to your account & \textbf{el cargo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El precio} is a number on a label. \emph{El coste} is what the thing ends up costing once postage and the rest are in — which is why a business talks about \emph{costes} and a shop window shows \emph{precios}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{constare}: \textbf{con-}, together, plus \textbf{stare}, \textbf{to stand}.

\emph{Constare} meant to stand firm, to be settled — and from \textquotedblleft{}this is settled\textquotedblright{} it became \textquotedblleft{}this is what it comes to\textquotedblright{}. The price is the point at which the matter stands still.

English took the same verb twice. Through French it wore down to \textbf{cost}; lifted straight from Latin it gave \textbf{constant}, a thing that stands firm. \emph{Coste} and \emph{constant} are one word, and you can hear the \emph{n} that Spanish dropped and English kept.

The \emph{stare} underneath is the one inside \textbf{estar}, and that is the sense to hold: a cost is a standing, a place the reckoning comes to rest.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the total cost, and at no extra cost
  \item the verb that goes with it
  \item which of \emph{precio} and \emph{coste} is on a price tag
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The cost? (\textbf{El coste}.) What does \emph{constare} mean? (\textbf{To stand firm}.) Which English word kept the \emph{n}? (\textbf{Constant}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la agencia]{la agencia — somebody who acts for you}

\label{lesson:ES-C456-agencia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la agenda} and \textbf{la oficina}. One of those two is about to turn out to be a relative.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la agencia}
\textbf{la agencia} — the agency.

\emph{Una agencia de viajes} — a travel agency. \emph{La agencia inmobiliaria} — the estate agent's. \emph{Lo he reservado por agencia} — I booked it through an agency.

\textbf{El agente} is the person. And the thing an agency charges you for its trouble is \textbf{la comisión}, which appears on the bill beside the \emph{coste}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -encia names the doing, again}]
You have a set of noun-making endings now, and this is another:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
-anza & la mudanza \\
-miento & el seguimiento \\
-encia & la agencia \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-encia} and its twin \textbf{-ancia} come off Latin present participles, which is why they so often name an activity or a quality: \emph{la paciencia}, \emph{la distancia}, \emph{la experiencia}, \emph{la importancia}.

Every \textbf{-encia} and \textbf{-ancia} noun is feminine. Set beside \emph{-anza}, \emph{-eza} and \emph{-ción}, that is five feminine suffix families against the masculine \emph{-miento}.

Keep the claim on the \textbf{suffixes}, though, not on abstract nouns in general — \emph{el coste} and \emph{el cargo} from this same chapter are masculine and end in neither. What the endings buy you is an article you no longer have to guess at, one ending at a time.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{agere}, \textbf{to do}, \textbf{to drive}, \textbf{to act}.

An \emph{agencia} is a place that \textbf{acts on your behalf}, and an \emph{agente} is the one doing the acting. Now look at \textbf{la agenda}, which you already have: it is \emph{agenda}, \textquotedblleft{}the things that must be done\textquotedblright{} — a Latin plural that Spanish took as a singular noun.

So your diary and a travel agency are the same verb: one lists what must be done, the other does it for you.

English is full of the family too — \textbf{agent}, \textbf{agenda}, \textbf{act}, \textbf{agile}, \textbf{agitate} — and Spanish keeps \emph{el acto}, \emph{la acción}, \emph{exigente} and \emph{ágil} off the same root.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a travel agency
  \item I booked it through an agency and the cost was higher
  \item what \emph{la agenda} literally means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The agency? (\textbf{La agencia}.) The person? (\textbf{El agente}.) What does \emph{agere} mean? (\textbf{To do, to act}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(la ensalada, el cargo, aceptar, el …]{(la ensalada, el cargo, aceptar, el coste, la agencia) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R456-repaso-cuenta}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{the salad}, \emph{the charge}, \emph{to accept}, \emph{the cost}, \emph{the agency}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three words for money on a page}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it names} & \textbf{the word} & \textbf{where you see it} \\
\midrule
what the seller asks & el precio & a label \\
what it comes to for you & el coste & a quote \\
what has been added & el cargo & a bill \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The order is the order of a transaction: you read a \emph{precio}, you work out a \emph{coste}, and afterwards a \emph{cargo} appears. Any of the three translated as \textquotedblleft{}price\textquotedblright{} will read as slightly wrong to a Spanish speaker in two of the three places.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four of the five were relatives}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new word} & \textbf{what it was built on} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la ensalada} & \emph{la sal} — the salted thing \\
\textbf{el cargo} & \emph{el carrito} — a load on a cart \\
\textbf{el coste} & \emph{costar}, and \emph{estar} underneath it \\
\textbf{la agencia} & \emph{la agenda} — things to be done \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La agencia} is the neat one. Your \textbf{agenda} is a Latin plural meaning \textquotedblleft{}the things that must be done\textquotedblright{}, and an \textbf{agencia} is a firm that does them for you. Diary and travel agent, one verb.

Even \textbf{aceptar} has one, though it takes longer to spot: its \emph{capere}, to take, is the \emph{capere} inside \textbf{el principio}, where \emph{princeps} is the one who \textbf{takes first place}. Every word in the chapter had a relative waiting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item there's a charge on the bill I didn't expect
  \item do you take card?
  \item which of the three money words appears last
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All five again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence querying something on a bill.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(revisar la cuenta) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C456-sintesis-cuenta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el cargo} and \textbf{la ensalada}. One of them is on the bill twice.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A bill on the table. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Mesa 7}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
2 \textbf{ensaladas} mixtas .......... 14,00
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
1 \textbf{ensalada} mixta ............ 7,00
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
2 cafés ......................... 3,60
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Cargo} por servicio .......... 2,50
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
No se \textbf{aceptan} tarjetas.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what has been counted twice, and what it should say
  \item what the 2,50 is for
  \item how you are going to have to pay
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
To query this politely you need the right noun, and it is \textbf{cargo} rather than \emph{precio}: the 2,50 was not asked for in advance, it was added. \emph{Hay un cargo que no entiendo} is the sentence, and \emph{hay un precio que no entiendo} would sound as though you were confused by the menu.

\textbf{No se aceptan tarjetas} is the \emph{se} construction again, and it is plural because \emph{tarjetas} is. Spanish agrees the verb with the thing, not with the restaurant, so a single line telling you the same thing about one card would read \emph{no se acepta tarjeta}.

A useful softener for the whole exchange: \emph{perdone, ¿me lo mira?} — literally \textquotedblleft{}will you look at it for me\textquotedblright{}, and far more common than accusing anybody of an error.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines querying a bill: ask them to look at it, say there is a charge you do not understand, say the salad appears twice, and ask whether they take card.

Then check yourself: did you use \emph{cargo} rather than \emph{precio}, and did \emph{se aceptan} agree with the cards?
\end{tcolorbox}
